**How Tensor Parallelism Splits a Transformer Across Two GPUs**
Tensor parallelism partitions the weight matrices of each transformer layer directly across devices. For example, in a multi-head attention (MHA) layer with 8 heads on two GPUs, GPU0 holds heads 0–3 and GPU1 holds heads 4–7. Similarly, for the feed-forward network (FFN), the first linear layer’s weight matrix \(W_1\) is split column-wise: each GPU stores half the columns. The second FFN linear layer \(W_2\) is then split row-wise to match the output dimension. During forward pass, each GPU computes its portion independently using local data shards.

**Why All-Reduce Is Needed After Each Layer**
After computing partial results—e.g., GPU0 produces head outputs 0–3 while GPU1 produces heads 4–7—neither device has the complete result required by the next layer (layer normalization or subsequent MHA/FFN). To reconstruct the full output, an **all-reduce** operation sums the partial contributions from both GPUs so that every GPU ends up with the identical, correct total. Without this synchronization, each GPU would hold only a fragment, breaking the sequential dependency between layers.

**All-Reduce Overhead and Optimization**
The all-reduce step introduces communication overhead equal to the size of the hidden state per token (e.g., 4096 floats per sequence position). This must occur after *every* MHA and FFN computation within each transformer block. While necessary for correctness, it can be partially overlapped with computation via pipelining or fused kernels. In practice, tensor parallelism scales well when model dimensions are large relative to batch size, as the communication cost grows linearly with hidden size but not with batch count.
